title: Sold Another Story
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reviews the second season of Emily Hanford's Sold a Story podcast, which widens its focus from early reading instruction to teaching in general by profiling Siegfried "Zig" Engelmann and his Direct Instruction model. She agrees with Hanford that American education has vastly undervalued explicit instruction, pointing to Project Follow Through, where Direct Instruction outperformed 21 other models yet was never named the winner. She compares Engelmann, who focused on how to teach and on language, with E.D. Hirsch, who focused on what to teach and on content knowledge. Wexler worries that listeners will conclude Direct Instruction alone fixes everything, that poor children need only basic facts, and that decontextualized comprehension-skills instruction (itself a form of lower-case direct instruction) will be reinforced. Her conclusion is that the two approaches, applied together, would be far more powerful than either alone.
points: Season 2 of Sold a Story argues that an education outsider, Engelmann, was right about teaching, and that the profession ignored the evidence from Project Follow Through because it contradicted its beliefs about discovery and inquiry.
Engelmann and Hirsch diagnosed the same achievement gap but prescribed differently: Engelmann emphasised how to teach and language, while Hirsch emphasised what to teach and background knowledge.
Wexler warns that explicit instruction applied to decontextualised comprehension strategies has caused real harm, because comprehension depends on knowledge rather than transferable skill.
She cautions against the idea that poor children need only basic facts and drilling, since all students eventually need to analyse and elaborate on what they learn.
Her synthesis is that Engelmann's method and Hirsch's content-rich curriculum should be used in tandem, not as rival answers.
quotes: Engelmann believed that if children weren’t learning, the problem was the teaching. He worked primarily with kids from low-income families and got extraordinary results.
Education orthodoxy holds that students, and especially young children, learn best through experience, discovery, and inquiry. Project Follow Through seemed to prove the opposite.
Knowledge and language are of course related, and both are important, but they’re not exactly the same. And some language, like the word or, is not particularly academic.
lots of evidence shows that direct instruction works better than inquiry or discovery when learners are new to a topic.
Typical comprehension instruction ignores that evidence. It has also crowded out knowledge-building subjects like social studies, especially in schools where reading scores are low.
Comprehension skills aren’t truly transferable. It’s easy, for example, to make an inference about a text if you have a lot of background knowledge relating to the topic.
Both Engelmann and Hirsch had keen insights about what has been missing from American education, with Engelmann focusing on how to teach and Hirsch on what to teach.
